articles.title: Dev log #2: nationwide data, typo-proof search, and a subway bug that picked a train 2 hours later
articles.description: A follow-up to my first post. I'm an 11th grader in Korea building OWN SHARK solo: an assistant that tells you what's open near you, ranked by real walking time. Here's what landed in the last three days. The subway bug: answering with a train 2 hours later For subway legs I call Seoul Metro's shortest-path API. I only asked for the "shortest travel time" search type. Sometimes the shortest ride was a train leaving two hours from now, so the app proudly recommended it. The fix: ask all three search types (duration, fewest transfers, distance) for the time you'd actually reach the station, then keep whichever arrives first. Wait time for the first train is added in, and if it's over 10 minutes the reply says so. If the API has no answer, the app says the ride time isn't confirmed instead of guessing. From Seoul to the whole country Places, place names and addresses now cover all of Korea. The government business list is fetched per province every week, with a checkpoint per page so a dropped connection resumes where it stopped. A run that comes back with less than half the previous rows is refused rather than wiping data. Typo-proof name search SQLite FTS5 trigram indexes over place names. A one-syllable typo still finds the school, and you can type only the initial consonants (초성, e.g. "ㄱㄴㅇ"). Exact matches always rank above fuzzy ones. The big indexes are built by a startup job, never inside a request. Closing shops that shut down Shop records are matched to the government business-licence data, but only when the building and the name both match. If the licence says closed, the shop is closed. If more than 5% of one category would flip in a single run, nothing changes and the run is flagged for a human. For visitors Answers in Japanese, Chinese and Vietnamese, not only Korean and English Incheon Airport: taxi stands, airport buses, gates, and live departure-hall queues from the airport's own API A paperwork-deadline helper for foreign residents, built from the immigration statute text; every answer cites the article and points to the official 1345 hotline Smaller things A 3D walking view: three.js buildings and a route ribbon inside MapLibre "Text mom I'm running late" opens the SMS screen with the text filled in. The user presses send A per-user monthly AI cost cap. Past it, the assistant falls back to rule-based answers Biggest lesson this round: don't take one API's answer as the truth. Both the subway bug and the closed shops were fixed by checking against a second source. Still pre-launch. Feedback very welcome. Waitlist (Korean page, 1 month free at launch): https://kqts5p68vrcer3-8000.proxy.runpod.net/pre?src=devto2

articles.title: Project500: what 105 ranked sets showed about an objective-first controller
articles.description: Disclosure: This post was written with Codex and is intended for the Battle.training Bot Bounty, which may pay up to $15 if accepted. Project500 is a JavaScript controller entered in the November Cup. Its first version, v1-objectives, uses terrain flow fields for routing and assigns the APC to contest objectives. What the ladder showed At the 105-set snapshot, Project500 recorded 46 wins, 44 losses, and 15 draws in the Cup, with a rating of 1239. Its public-ladder rating at that snapshot was 1334 across 61 sets. These are separate leaderboards, so the numbers should not be combined into a single win rate. A replay to inspect In this ranked set, Project500 won 2–0. The first game ended with the hill locked. The replay makes it possible to inspect which units reached the objective and when, while the standings show how the controller performed across opponents. For the next iteration, I would compare objective arrival times in wins and losses before changing the routing weights. One replay can generate a hypothesis, but it cannot establish which part of the controller caused a win. Public bot record and ranked-set data.

articles.title: What I learned building 700+ browser-only tools (no uploads, ever)
articles.description: I run theomnikit.com, a free site with 700+ small tools: PDF, image, video, developer utilities and calculators. Every file tool runs in the visitor's browser. Nothing is uploaded, and that one rule decided most of the engineering. This is what I learned getting there, including the parts that broke. I wrote this with AI help and checked every claim against the code and the project's decision log. The rule, and how it is enforced The first architecture decision was "browser-only; any server-side processing needs a new decision". A rule in a doc is easy to break quietly, so it is enforced by a test: no API route accepts a file (no multipart parser, no upload interceptor); nginx refuses any request body over 1 MB; the API's JSON parser stops at 1 MB. There is exactly one exception, and it has its own written decision: a screenshot attached to a bug report, redrawn on a canvas into a JPEG of at most 600 KB, so camera and location metadata never leave the device. One thing I got wrong early: I listed OCR as "out of scope" because I assumed it needed a server. It was the upload I had ruled out, not the reading of text. Image to Text now runs tesseract.js as WebAssembly. Because the CSP is connect-src 'self' and every Tesseract default points at a CDN, the worker, cores and language files are served from our own domain. How a file tool actually works The flow is the same everywhere: the File API hands over the bytes, the format is detected from the bytes (not the extension), the heavy library is fetched as soon as the file arrives, and the job runs when the person taps one button that names the action. Long jobs go to a Web Worker. The PDF tools, such as Grayscale PDF, share a small runner: one worker per tool, created on first use, the ArrayBuffer transferred rather than copied, progress posted back, and a fallback to the main thread when a worker cannot start. Workers are also a safety valve. The Regex Tester builds its worker from the same function the unit tests cover, and terminates it after 2 seconds, because a pattern that needs longer is almost always backtracking catastrophically. But a worker is not a fix for a bad algorithm. The diff checker froze on large inputs; moving it to a worker would have stopped the freeze and still failed the same comparisons. It got a better alignment algorithm with a time budget instead. Video without ffmpeg.wasm Video was where browser-only nearly broke. Single-threaded ffmpeg.wasm re-encoded a 5-minute 1080p video in 35 to 90 minutes. The multithreaded build needs SharedArrayBuffer, which means COOP/COEP headers, which blank out third-party ads, so that was not an option for a free site. The video tools, like Trim Video, use WebCodecs with mp4box and mp4-muxer instead: about 50 KB gzipped against ffmpeg's 32 MB. Trimming copies the original frames when the shape stays the same, so a short clip finishes in under a second with no quality loss. The pitfalls nobody warns you about iOS Safari's canvas limit. Safari refuses a canvas over about 16.7 megapixels, and recent iPhones shoot 24 MP by default. The failure is not even consistent: sometimes no context, sometimes an InvalidStateError on encode. Image to PDF now caps every encode at 16.7 MP, retries at half the pixels down to 2 MP, and tries a DOM canvas when OffscreenCanvas refuses. Thumbnails are full photos. Forty 12 MP photos in a preview strip is about 2 GB of decoded pixels on a phone. Thumbnails are now 480 px JPEGs made when the file is added. HEIC. One image tool accepted HEIC and handed it straight to createImageBitmap, so every HEIC failed in Chrome and Firefox, which cannot decode it. The image tools now share one loader that handles HEIC, and HEIC to JPG decodes with a dedicated library in the browser. Memory on big files. Before decoding an image, a pixel guard reads width and height from the first 256 KB and refuses an oversized image with a clear message. Running out of memory is reported as "too large for this browser", never as "damaged file", because it says nothing about the file. PDF limits, such as on Compress PDF, were deliberately not raised until browser memory is actually measured. Feature probes that lie. Every "to WebP" page once told visitors their browser could not write WebP, in a browser that could. The probe encoded a 1x1 OffscreenCanvas that had never had a rendering context, and that throws for every format. Test the probe, not just the feature. Why every tool is its own page Each tool has its own URL, title, short answer at the top and structured data, because the site has no marketing budget: people arrive from search engines and AI assistants asking one specific question, and the page has to be the answer. That also has a limit. Of 151 landing variants Google left "discovered, not indexed", 108 were folded into their parent with a 301. One page per real search intent, not one per keyword. State lives in the URL too. When one tool suggests the next step (say, compress the PDF you just made), the plan travels as link parameters, and the file is handed over in memory. No account, no server-side history. The standard that ties it together The bar for a file tool is two taps on a phone: choose the file, confirm. Zero scrolls. The site never runs a job on a dropped file by itself; that one confirmation is what makes "your files never leave your device" believable. If you are building something similar: write the no-upload rule down, enforce it with a test, put long jobs in workers, and test on a real iPhone early. Most of my bugs were in that last one.

articles.title: Part 32: Data residency and on-prem runtimes compared
articles.description: Part 32 · One Agent, Five Platforms Regulated? Then where the agent and its data run matters as much as what it does. An invoice agent reads supplier bank details, approval history and amounts. A security or data protection review will ask three questions before it asks anything about prompts: Runtime: where does the agent itself run, and can it run in our own infrastructure? Model: where are prompts and completions processed? Logs: where do traces, conversation history and audit records end up? Part 30 flagged residency as the control with the most gaps. This part answers the three questions for each platform, from vendor documentation I read on 20 November 2026. Like the builds, it's documentation-only, and the gaps are stated rather than filled. MuleSoft Runtime. Agent networks deploy to a CloudHub 2.0 shared or private space, or a Runtime Fabric target. Runtime Fabric runs on infrastructure you manage, so it's the customer-hosted option (Part 11). The control planes overview lists agent network projects and the LLM gateway as available on the EU control plane. Since 16 November 2026, the release notes also list Hyperforce as a target for version 2.0 agent networks. Model. The broker calls an LLM provider you configure, through the gateway. I found no statement about where those calls are processed. That depends on the provider and region you choose. Logs. Traces and logs go to Anypoint Monitoring, and the EU control plane lists log search, raw log data and a telemetry exporter. Retention and storage location weren't on the pages I read. Boomi Runtime. The runtime clouds page lists four Boomi-managed clouds: US East, UK, Japan and Australia. There's still no EU cloud; the UK one is outside the EU. A self-hosted Flex runtime "runs in your own infrastructure" but is in early access, as it was in Part 15. Model. The Boomi AI FAQ says agents use models through Amazon Bedrock, and that each runtime runs the model, prompts and responses "in the selected region". You can also connect your own Anthropic, OpenAI or Google account, in which case prompts go to that provider. On Flex, "only the model prompt leaves your network". Logs. Audit trace logs are in Agent Control Tower, without a stated retention period. Chat sessions are kept until a user deletes them. Two exceptions matter for residency: glossary and knowledge base content is stored in the platform's region, so a North America customer running agents in the UK, Japan or Australia retrieves it from the US. SAP Runtime. The Business AI reference architecture says the platform is "SAP-managed by default", with SAP AI Core running on AWS, Azure and Google Cloud. SAP Learning's data residency lesson describes locally hosted AI, SAP Sovereign Cloud and an EU AI Cloud with "AI infrastructure hosted within Europe". I found no on-premises option for Joule agents, and no availability dates for those offerings. Model. Models come through the generative AI hub, from SAP and partners such as Anthropic, OpenAI, Mistral and Cohere. The lesson says processing "may occur on SAP-managed infrastructure or approved external model providers, depending on the use case and configuration". I found no way to pin Joule's model calls to a region. Logs. Not covered in what I read, as in Part 18. The architecture mentions agent session telemetry going to SAP Cloud ALM, but not where it's stored or for how long. Azure Runtime. Foundry Agent Service endpoints are regional, and the FAQ says "data is stored in the same region as the endpoint". In the standard setup, threads, files and vector stores go to your own Cosmos DB, Storage and AI Search resources. Agents can run in your virtual network, on a delegated subnet in the same region. There's no on-premises option on these pages. Model. This is where Azure is clearest. The deployment types page defines three levels: Global: may be processed in any Azure region. Data Zone: processed only within the US, EU or APAC zone. The EU zone is the EU Data Boundary. Standard (regional): processed within the geography you choose. In every case, "data stored at rest remains in the designated Azure geography". So the deployment type you pick is a residency decision, not just a pricing one. Logs. Traces go to an Application Insights resource in your own subscription (Part 22). AWS Runtime. AgentCore Runtime, Gateway, Identity and Observability are available in seven European regions, according to the regions page: Frankfurt, Ireland, London, Milan, Paris, Spain and Stockholm. Milan and Spain don't have Memory or Runtime Instances yet. The runtime can attach to your VPC (Part 25). There's no on-premises option. Model. Bedrock's geographic cross-Region inference keeps EU requests within EU regions. But prompts and results "might move outside of your source Region", and any abuse-detection copies are stored in the destination region. On the AgentCore side, the cross-Region inference page says Memory, Policy and Evaluations use it. From the EU regions it stays in Europe. From some other source regions, Policy and Evaluations use global routing that can leave the geography. Logs. Observability writes to CloudWatch in your account (Part 25). The cross-Region page warns that CloudWatch and CloudTrail logs "won't specify the AWS Region in which data inference occurs". What the builds could and could not show Could: where each vendor says the runtime runs, which regions exist, and which platforms offer a customer-hosted runtime. MuleSoft has Runtime Fabric, and Boomi has Flex in early access. Could not: where model calls actually land for MuleSoft and SAP, and log retention on most of them. Those need the vendor's trust documentation or contract terms, and a hands-on build that checks the traces. For an EU-only requirement: Azure's Data Zone and AWS's EU regions are the most explicit in the docs. MuleSoft can keep the runtime and control plane in the EU but leaves model location to your provider. Boomi has no EU-managed cloud. SAP describes an EU AI Cloud without dates I could find. The policy from Part 30 still holds: classify the data first, then pick the runtime, model deployment and log store that keep each class where it's allowed. Where must your agent data stay? This series describes a reference build on a fictional company. This part is based only on vendor documentation read on 20 November 2026 and the documentation-only builds in Parts 11 to 30; no hands-on build has been run yet. It's not legal or compliance advice. Views are my own.

articles.title: Healthtech Background Job Queue: Fixing Malformed 256KB JSON Payloads
articles.description: Short answer: keep the renewal command small, validate the serialized bytes and schema in both the Node.js producer and consumer, and store the large health record outside the queue behind a stable reference. The 256 KB ceiling is a contract boundary, not a retryable incident; malformed JSON and schema failures should be quarantined with an audit record, while a delayed reminder should be recoverable through idempotent consumer state. This matters when a healthtech business wants to delay a renewal reminder until a contract or business deadline. The reminder is time-sensitive, but its payload should not become a copy of the subscription, patient, or billing aggregate. A queue message should say what must happen, when the decision was made, and where the worker can obtain the minimum authorized input. How should a background job queue reject malformed 256KB payloads? Treat the producer and consumer as two independent contract boundaries. The producer creates an explicit envelope, serializes it once, measures the resulting byte length, and refuses a message above 256 KB. The consumer performs the same byte check before parsing, then parses JSON, validates the schema, checks domain rules, and only then starts the reminder workflow. Repeating validation is deliberate: a delayed message may outlive a deployment, and another publishing path may not share the producer's assumptions. The order prevents confusing failures. A byte-limit violation is not a JSON parse error. A malformed document is not a schema violation. A syntactically valid object can still lack a message ID, a deadline, a schema version, or the reference needed to decide whether a reminder is still appropriate. Log those classifications separately; otherwise an operations dashboard will describe three different contract failures as one mysterious retry spike. The practical envelope for this scenario is small: type RenewalReminder struct { SchemaVersion int `json:"schema_version"` MessageID string `json:"message_id"` AccountID string `json:"account_id"` Deadline string `json:"business_deadline"` Subscription string `json:"subscription_ref"` Template string `json:"template_version"` } The reference is not automatically harmless. In a healthtech system, an account ID or subscription reference can still be personal data, so it belongs in the deletion inventory and access-control model. GDPR Article 17 does not stop applying because the identifier moved from an HTTP request into a queue or a database table. The architecture decision record: where does recovery stop? The decision is to use a versioned command envelope, a durable inbox, and a separate source for large objects. The invariants are more important than the queue brand: A message is accepted only if its serialized bytes are at or below 256 KB. The schema version, command identity, business deadline, and reference are required. The consumer records the message ID before the reminder side effect, using a uniqueness constraint in the same transaction as the business state transition. An acknowledgement follows the committed transaction, not the moment the worker begins processing. A permanent contract failure is recorded and quarantined; a transient delivery failure can be retried within a bounded policy. This is an exactly-once mindset applied where it can actually be enforced. A queue may deliver a message more than once. The application can still make the business effect happen once by putting the inbox insert and the reminder-state update in one database transaction. If the worker crashes after the transaction commits but before acknowledgement, redelivery finds the existing message ID and does not send a second reminder. The audit row should include the message ID, schema version, correlation ID, disposition, timestamp, and a digest of the received bytes. It generally should not include the raw health record or the entire JSON body. A digest lets an investigator connect a repeated failure to an input without spreading another copy of regulated data through logs. Recovery becomes much clearer when the producer's refusal and the consumer's quarantine are treated as different observations. A producer can reject a message before it leaves the application, which is the cheapest place to expose a growing payload and the best place to return a useful validation error to the caller. A consumer, by contrast, has to assume that the message may have been emitted by an older release, replayed from a redrive tool, or produced by a second service that did not share the current schema package. It therefore records what it actually received, including the byte count and digest, rather than copying the producer's explanation. During an investigation, those two records answer different questions: did the publishing path understand the contract, and did the worker enforce the contract at the point of side effect? Keeping both answers makes an audit trail useful without making the queue a second patient-record system. It also gives an operator a controlled repair path: correct the producer, deploy the schema change, inspect quarantined IDs, and redrive only messages whose business deadlines and authorization still make them valid. Keep it boring. Decision area Compact command envelope Full aggregate in the message Size control Easy to measure before publish Can cross 256 KB as fields grow Schema change Versioned command contract Couples the worker to unrelated fields Privacy Keeps routine copies out of the queue Replicates sensitive fields into queue retention Recovery Redrive one command after fixing the cause Reconstruct and re-authorize a large object Appropriate use Renewal decision and stable reference A small, self-contained, non-sensitive object The rejected option is compression as the primary fix. Compression may reduce transport bytes, but it does not solve schema coupling, retention, access control, or a consumer that parses an unexpected version. Fragmenting one large object is worse for recovery: now operators must reconcile missing pieces, duplicate fragments, ordering, expiration, and authorization at assembly time. There is a valid use for the full-object design. Use it when the object is demonstrably below the limit, has a stable versioned schema, contains no separately governed data, and has idempotent processing. That is a reasonable choice for a compact internal command. It is a poor default for an evolving healthtech aggregate. A Go reference implementation for the producer-consumer boundary The following sample shows the critical path without pretending that an in-memory map is a production inbox. The production version should put the uniqueness check, renewal-state change, and outbox or send decision under the database's transaction rules. The sample's useful property is its failure classification: oversize, malformed JSON, and invalid schema do not enter an endless retry loop. package main import ( "crypto/sha256" "encoding/hex" "encoding/json" "errors" "fmt" ) func validate(job RenewalReminder) error { if job. SchemaVersion != 1 { return fmt. Errorf("unsupported schema version: %d", job. SchemaVersion) if job. MessageID == "" || job. AccountID == "" || job. Deadline == "" || job. Subscription == "" || job. Template == "" { return errors. New("message_id, account_id, deadline, subscription_ref, and template_version are required") return nil func encodeForPublish(job RenewalReminder) ([]byte, error) { if err := validate(job); err != nil { return nil, fmt. Errorf("schema rejected before publish: %w", err) payload, err := json. Marshal(job) if err != nil { return nil, fmt. Errorf("JSON encoding failed: %w", err) if len(payload) > maxMessageBytes { return nil, fmt. Errorf("permanent size failure: %d bytes exceeds %d", len(payload), maxMessageBytes) return payload, nil func consume(payload []byte, inbox map[string]string) error { return fmt. Errorf("permanent size failure: %d bytes exceeds %d", len(payload), maxMessageBytes) var job RenewalReminder if err := json. Unmarshal(payload, &job); err != nil { return fmt. Errorf("permanent JSON failure: %w", err) return fmt. Errorf("permanent schema failure: %w", err) if priorDigest, exists := inbox[job. MessageID]; exists { digest := sha256. Sum256(payload) inbox[job. MessageID] = hex. EncodeToString(digest[:]) func main() { job := RenewalReminder{ SchemaVersion: 1, MessageID: "renewal-20260811-001", AccountID: "acct-4821", Deadline: "2026-08-15T17:00:00Z", Subscription: "sub-2048", Template: "renewal-v3", payload, err := encodeForPublish(job) panic(err) inbox := map[string]string{} if err := consume(payload, inbox); err != nil { The real Node.js implementation should preserve the same sequence even if its validation library differs: use a byte measurement of the encoded Buffer, not a character count; reject unknown schema versions; and keep the producer's error response distinct from the consumer's quarantine disposition. A JavaScript string length is not a reliable proxy for UTF-8 bytes when the payload contains non-ASCII data. One subtle healthtech rule belongs after validation but before sending: re-read the subscription state and compare it with the stored deadline and template policy. A renewal can be cancelled, paid, or moved while the message waits. The worker should record that decision as a normal terminal disposition, not send an old reminder because the queue message was technically valid. How can operators distinguish retryable delivery failures from contract failures? Use a small state machine rather than one generic failed flag. published means the producer passed local validation. received means the consumer obtained bytes. quarantined means the bytes or schema cannot produce a valid command. ready means the inbox transaction committed and the reminder is eligible for the deadline policy. sent means the external notification outcome was recorded. A separate cancelled or superseded state handles a subscription that changed while work was waiting. The retry rule follows the state, not the emotional urgency of the reminder. A broker connection interruption, temporary database unavailability, or notification provider timeout may be retriable with a finite attempt budget. Invalid JSON, an unsupported schema version, a missing reference, and a 256 KB violation are deterministic; retrying them creates noise and can delay valid work behind a poisoned message. A dead-letter or quarantine record should retain the message ID, error class, schema version if parseable, byte count, digest, and the producer release identifier. RabbitMQ's consumer acknowledgement documentation is useful here because acknowledgement timing is an explicit part of delivery semantics. A worker should acknowledge after durable application state is committed, and it should expect redelivery when the process ends before acknowledgement. The acknowledgement is not an audit record and cannot substitute for an inbox constraint. For a delayed reminder, recovery also requires visibility into time. Measure queue age, time until business deadline, quarantine count by error class, redelivery count, inbox duplicates, and the number of reminders superseded before sending. Alert on a deadline approaching with no ready state, not only on worker crashes. A healthy process can repeatedly reject every message and still look green if the only metric is process uptime. I once assumed the parse-error rate was the important signal in this class of system. It wasn't. The more useful question was how many valid reminders had less than an hour before their business deadline while waiting behind invalid work. That metric changed the recovery conversation from “the queue is noisy” to “these 18 accounts need an operator decision.” When is a different queue architecture the right choice? The compact command pattern is not a universal answer. A queue is a poor source of truth for compliance evidence, and a short retention window is not a replay archive. If the business requires long-lived event replay, independent consumer groups, or historical reconstruction, use an event-log design with explicit retention and deletion controls. If the workflow has many durable steps, timers, joins, or human approvals, a workflow engine may express recovery more clearly than a hand-built retry table. Stay with a simple queue when the job is one bounded command, the consumer owns an idempotency boundary, and operators can redrive quarantined messages after correcting the producer. Choose a workflow or event-log architecture when recovery requires reconstructing a sequence rather than repeating one command. The catch is operational ownership: each broader model adds retention, replay, permissions, and audit decisions that the team must test and document. The final decision rule is narrow. Put only the renewal intent and a controlled reference on the queue; make byte size and schema validation executable at both ends; commit idempotent state before acknowledgement; and keep compliance evidence in a durable system designed for audit and erasure. That's enough architecture to make a 256 KB failure boring, which is exactly what an operator needs at a business deadline. References RabbitMQ consumer acknowledgements: https://www.rabbitmq.com/docs/confirms GDPR Article 17, Right to erasure: https://gdpr-info.eu/art-17-gdpr/

articles.title: Mastering the Three Layers of Model Serving: An Architectural Breakdown of Philip Kiely's 'Inference Engineering'
articles.description: read the book: https://www.baseten.co/inference-engineering/book/ When ChatGPT launched on November 30, 2022, only a few hundred engineers worldwide possessed the specialized expertise required to serve large-scale generative AI models. In the years since, the rapid proliferation of open-weights foundation models has transformed model serving from an elite research operation into an essential engineering discipline. In Inference Engineering: Serving Generative AI in Production, published by Baseten Books, author Philip Kiely presents the definitive technical roadmap for this emerging field. Situated squarely between low-level GPU kernel development in CUDA and high-level cloud orchestration in Kubernetes, inference engineering is defined as the practice of serving generative models in production with strict bounds on latency, throughput, reliability, and cost-efficiency. While classic machine learning models like XGBoost ran efficiently on lightweight CPUs with minimal software overhead, generative AI models demand dedicated GPU clusters, complex memory layout optimizations, and specialized runtime engines. As Kiely establishes, a production-grade inference system relies on three tightly integrated layers: The Runtime Layer: Optimizes execution performance and VRAM efficiency for an individual model running on a single GPU or a multi-GPU instance. The Infrastructure Layer: Manages horizontal scaling, regional failover, and multi-cloud capacity to maintain high availability under fluctuating traffic spikes. The Tooling Layer: Delivers developer abstractions that balance granular hardware control against developer productivity. This comprehensive overview dissects the core concepts, hardware topologies, software engines, applied research techniques, and production deployment patterns detailed throughout Kiely's work. Prerequisites and Evals: Architectural Trade-Offs and SLA Benchmarking Before optimizing low-level kernels or provisioning GPU clusters, engineering teams must evaluate the strategic transition from shared API endpoints to dedicated infrastructure deployments. Shared inference APIs—such as those operated by frontier labs—offer immediate access with zero infrastructure overhead. However, as product usage scales, relying on generic endpoints introduces severe trade-offs, including unmanaged latency spikes, strict rate limits, lack of hardware visibility, and per-token pricing that scales linearly with volume. According to Kiely, shifting AI products to dedicated GPU deployments becomes imperative when organizations reach token volume thresholds where paying per GPU hour is substantially more economical than paying per million tokens, when privacy requirements prohibit third-party data transit, or when custom fine-tuned weights and lower latency percentiles are required. Operational Dimension Shared API Endpoints Dedicated GPU Deployments Cost Structure Linear cost scaling per token consumed Fixed hourly cost per provisioned GPU instance Infrastructure Overhead Zero maintenance; managed by vendor Requires containerization, routing, and cluster management Cold Starts & Availability Always available; zero warm-up time Requires warm instance pools and fast image loading Performance Control Constrained by vendor rate limits and noisy neighbors Full control over latency SLAs, batching, and GPU SKUs Data Privacy & Security Data transits external vendor infrastructure Complete data isolation within private cloud perimeters To determine whether dedicated model serving satisfies application constraints, inference engineers separate low-level model performance metrics from end-to-end system metrics: Metric Category Specific Indicator Operational Focus & Bottlenecks Model Inference Metrics Time to First Token (TTFT) Measures the compute-bound Prefill phase processing input sequences Tokens Per Second (TPS) Measures the memory-bandwidth-bound Decode phase emitting tokens System-Level Metrics End-to-End Latency Encompasses client overhead, network transit, model queueing, and generation P50 / P99 Latency Percentiles Tracks median experience against tail latency under heavy concurrency As emphasized in the text, high-conviction model evaluation (evals) is a mandatory prerequisite for inference engineering. Establishing standardized evaluation suites—using benchmarks like MMLU for general knowledge, GSM8K for mathematical reasoning, or SWE-bench for code generation—ensures that runtime optimizations like lossy quantization or aggressive speculative decoding do not compromise model intelligence. Hardware Accelerators and Interconnect Topologies Generative model performance is fundamentally bounded by physical hardware specs. Kiely's examination of datacenter accelerators focuses primarily on NVIDIA GPU architectures—spanning Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell generations—while assessing compute capacity and memory bandwidth dynamics. Modern datacenter GPUs integrate Streaming Multiprocessors (SMs) for mathematical computation alongside High-Bandwidth Memory (HBM). Evaluating accelerator spec sheets requires balancing raw FLOPS against memory bandwidth: Memory Bandwidth: The primary bottleneck during autoregressive token generation. Accelerators like the NVIDIA H100 SXM offer high memory bandwidth to rapidly move model weights into compute cores, while Blackwell B200 GPUs expand bandwidth up to 8 TB/s. Tensor Cores and Precision Formats: Hardware units engineered for matrix multiplication. Recent generations introduce hardware support for FP8 and FP4 precisions, as well as microscaling formats (MXFP8 and MXFP4), significantly boosting throughput. Interconnect Speed: High-speed GPU-to-GPU channels like NVLink (delivering up to 900 GB/s on Hopper and 1800 GB/s on Blackwell) and NVSwitch allow multiple accelerators within a single chassis to act as a unified memory pool. When serving small models whose parameters do not saturate a large accelerator's capacity, allocating a full datacenter GPU results in wasted compute. In these cases, Multi-Instance GPU (MIG) technology enables physical GPUs (such as the A100 or H100) to be partitioned at the silicon level into up to seven isolated hardware instances, complete with dedicated SM compute slices, memory, and bus bandwidth. Conversely, for non-NVIDIA datacenter hardware, specialized alternatives target specific operational edges: startups like Groq and Cerebras prioritize ultra-high-bandwidth memory for rapid decode, while vendors like Qualcomm and Furiosa focus on power efficiency. The Software Abstraction Hierarchy: CUDA to High-Performance Inference Engines The inference software stack transforms physical silicon into flexible serving environments. As detailed in the text, inference software operates across four ascending levels of abstraction: CUDA Kernels: Direct GPU programming for low-level memory and compute management. Fused CUDA kernels—such as FlashAttention for memory-efficient attention and DeepGEMM for FP8 matrix operations—drastically reduce memory accesses by keeping intermediate activations in fast GPU SRAM. Deep Learning Frameworks: Libraries like PyTorch provide Python-level constructs for execution graphs and tensor operations, supported by serialization formats like Safetensors. Inference Engines: Highly optimized serving frameworks—including vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM—that implement continuous batching, dynamic KV cache allocation, and performance optimizations. Distributed Orchestrators: Enterprise infrastructure systems such as NVIDIA Dynamo that manage disaggregated, multi-node deployments across large GPU clusters. Choosing the right inference engine depends on the organization's requirements for model flexibility, deployment speed, and hardware optimization: Inference Engine Key Technical Characteristics Optimal Production Use Case vLLM High community adoption, broad architecture coverage, day-zero model support General-purpose serving of diverse open LLMs and visual models SGLang Advanced Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) support, Multi-Latent Attention (MLA) optimization High-throughput serving of frontier open architectures (e.g., DeepSeek) TensorRT-LLM Custom engine compilation, deep NVIDIA hardware fusion Maximum throughput on static, high-volume production deployments To validate software choices, inference engineers utilize benchmarking and load testing tools such as genai-bench and GenAI-Perf to simulate real-world request concurrency and sequence lengths. Applied Optimization Techniques for Production Models Chapter 5 of Kiely's work outlines five core applied research techniques used to accelerate inference and maximize throughput. 4.1 Quantization Quantization lowers the numerical precision of model weights, activations, or KV cache tensors from 16-bit floating point (FP16/BF16) down to FP8, INT8, or FP4. This reduces overall VRAM footprint, relieves memory bandwidth bottlenecks, and increases matrix multiplication speed on specialized Tensor Cores. While lossless techniques preserve exact model quality, aggressive quantization schemes require evaluating cosine similarity or task accuracy to ensure quality remains intact. For edge and local deployment, formats like GGUF provide quantized model distribution across resource-constrained environments. 4.2 Speculative Decoding Autoregressive decoding generates tokens sequentially, leaving GPU compute cores underutilized at small batch sizes because the entire weight matrix must be loaded from memory for every single token. Speculative decoding overcomes this by using a lightweight draft mechanism—such as a smaller companion draft model or EAGLE heads—to generate a sequence of draft tokens quickly. A larger target model then validates the draft tokens in a single parallel forward pass, accepting correct tokens and resampling upon mismatch. For structured text like code completion, n-gram speculation extracts repeated token sequences directly from prompt context without requiring a draft model. 4.3 KV Cache Reuse and Prefix Caching During token generation, self-attention requires retaining Key and Value states for all preceding tokens in memory as a KV cache. For extended context windows, the KV cache quickly exceeds the memory size of the model weights themselves. Prefix caching reuses pre-computed KV cache blocks across requests sharing identical system prompts or reference documents. Additionally, Chunked Prefill breaks long input sequences into smaller chunks, allowing heavy prefill computations to be scheduled alongside active decode loops without causing latency spikes. 4.4 Model Parallelism Strategies When a model is too large to fit inside a single GPU's VRAM, its execution must be parallelized across multiple accelerators using targeted strategies: Tensor Parallelism (TP): Splits individual matrix multiplication operations across multiple GPUs within a node. TP minimizes token generation latency but requires ultra-high-bandwidth NVLink interconnects. Pipeline Parallelism (PP): Partitions sequential model layers across GPUs or nodes, introducing micro-batch pipeline execution to minimize idle GPU time. Expert Parallelism (EP): Tailored for Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures, EP routes tokens to specialized expert layers residing on different GPUs while replicating shared self-attention blocks, achieving high throughput with lower inter-GPU communication requirements. When scaling across multiple physical server nodes connected via InfiniBand, hybrid configurations like TP8PP2 (Tensor Parallelism within nodes, Pipeline Parallelism across nodes) or EP16 optimize communication topology for massive workloads. 4.5 Disaggregated Serving (Disaggregation) LLM inference involves two distinct execution phases: the compute-heavy Prefill phase (processing the prompt and generating the first token) and the memory-bound Decode phase (generating subsequent tokens one by one). Running both phases on the same GPU instance under high concurrency leads to resource contention. Disaggregated serving separates these workloads onto specialized GPU workers through a structured sequence: Prefill Processing: Dedicated prefill workers ingest the input prompt, compute the initial KV cache, and output the first token. KV Cache Transfer: The prefill worker transfers the generated KV cache over high-speed interconnects to a decode worker. Decode Autoregression: The decode worker executes the remaining generation steps using memory-optimized configurations. Systems like NVIDIA Dynamo manage these setups dynamically using configurable worker ratios, denoted as x\text{P}y\text{D} (e.g., 5 Prefill workers paired with 3 Decode workers), allowing systems to adjust worker allocations in real time as traffic conditions evolve. Multi-Modal Inference: Vision, Speech, and Diffusion Architectures Inference engineering extends beyond text-based LLMs to encompass vision, audio, and visual generation modalities: Vision-Language Models (VLMs): Integrate image encoders with autoregressive text backbones. Because vision tokens extend prompt lengths, prefix caching for image embeddings and EAGLE speculative decoding are vital for maintaining low latency. Speech and ASR Pipelines: Real-time voice processing pairs Voice Activity Detection (VAD) with transcription models (like Whisper) and speech synthesis decoders (like SNAC). Performance is evaluated using the Real-Time Factor (RTF), requiring independent microservice autoscaling across pipeline stages. Image and Video Diffusion Models: Unlike autoregressive models, diffusion models generate outputs through iterative denoising loops. Serving diffusion pipelines involves coordinating text encoders, denoising Transformers, and Variational Autoencoders (VAEs), where CUDA kernel fusion and TensorRT compilation deliver primary performance gains. Production Operations, Infrastructure, and Multi-Cloud Scaling Operating performant inference services at scale requires dedicated infrastructure discipline. Chapter 7 details the operational requirements for building reliable, production-grade model serving platforms: 6.1 Containerization and Weight Caching Model serving environments are standardized using container technologies such as Docker or packaged NVIDIA Inference Microservices (NIMs). Because AI container images span tens of gigabytes due to CUDA dependencies, PyTorch libraries, and model engines, mitigating cold start latency requires caching model weights on high-speed local NVMe storage or utilizing fast intra-datacenter network transfers. 6.2 Multi-Cloud Capacity and Geo-Aware Routing Due to global GPU supply constraints, enterprise deployments often span heterogeneous GPU pools across multiple cloud providers (hyperscalers and neoclouds). A resilient multi-cloud architecture separates a global control plane from regional workload planes: Global Control Plane: Performs geo-aware load balancing, routing user traffic to the nearest healthy cluster with available GPU capacity and low queue depth. Regional Workload Planes: Isolated clusters running model replicas across reserved, on-demand, and spot GPU instances, managed by autoscaling policies operating on target concurrency and TTFT/TPS SLAs. 6.3 Transitioning Unit Economics Shifting from third-party APIs to dedicated GPU infrastructure changes cost accounting from variable per-token charges to fixed hourly instance costs. Maximizing economic efficiency requires driving up GPU utilization through dynamic batching, disaggregated serving, and multi-tenant bin packing. Strategic Takeaways and Continuing Education Philip Kiely's Inference Engineering: Serving Generative AI in Production establishes that achieving fast, cost-effective, and reliable AI serving requires holistic optimization across the entire stack. By mastering runtime techniques, engine selection, and distributed infrastructure, engineering teams can build resilient AI platforms capable of scaling open models in production. For practitioners seeking to deepen their technical expertise, Kiely highlights three essential companion texts in Appendix B: AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models by Chip Huyen (O'Reilly Media, 2025): A comprehensive exploration of the broader AI application lifecycle. Build a Large Language Model (From Scratch) by Sebastian Raschka (Manning, 2024): A detailed, code-first breakdown of transformer neural network architectures. AI Systems Performance Engineering by Chris Fregly (O'Reilly Media, 2025): An in-depth guide to low-level GPU, CUDA, and PyTorch performance tuning.

articles.title: Why I Built a macOS Cmd-Tab Switcher Without Screen Recording Permission (Swift 6 + AppKit)
articles.description: If you regularly keep 20+ apps open on macOS—editors, terminals, browsers, chat apps, notes—the built-in ⌘-Tab switcher starts to break down fast: You have to tap Tab over and over to reach an app buried in the middle of the row. You can't jump straight to a specific window of an app (or a specific terminal tab). If an app's windows are minimized, ⌘-Tab focuses the menu bar and leaves you staring at an empty desktop. Open-source tools like AltTab solve the window problem well by bringing Windows-style live thumbnails to macOS. There's just one catch: rendering live thumbnails of other apps' windows requires the system-wide Screen Recording permission—which on macOS 15 Sequoia also triggers recurring monthly OS re-confirmation prompts and menu bar indicators. I wanted a switcher that stayed fast at 20+ apps without ever asking to record my screen. So I built AbcTab in pure Swift 6 + AppKit around a different trade-off. 1. The Core Trade-off: Skip Thumbnails, Optimize for Muscle Memory When you have 4 or 5 windows open, scanning live thumbnails is intuitive. When you have 20+ apps and browser windows open, visually scanning a grid of tiny previews actually slows you down. Instead of capturing pixels, AbcTab focuses on icons + first-letter badges + readable window/tab titles: First-letter jump (English + Chinese Pinyin): Hold ⌘-Tab and tap C for Code, G for Ghostty, O for Obsidian, or W for WeChat (matching Pinyin initials automatically without switching input sources). MRU cycling on collisions: When multiple apps share the same initial (e.g., Chrome and Ghostty both under G), tap the same letter again to cycle through them in Most-Recently-Used order. Zero Screen Recording permission: Because AbcTab never captures window pixels, it only uses standard macOS Accessibility APIs to enumerate window titles, raise target windows across Spaces, and restore minimized windows. 2. Expanding Windows and Terminal Tabs (Including Ghostty) For apps with multiple windows—or terminals that expose tabs cleanly such as Ghostty—staying on an app icon (or pressing ↓) expands a high-density list of window and tab titles right below the icon: In day-to-day coding, readable project names and terminal titles are almost always faster to recognize than a downscaled screenshot of two dark-mode editors. 3. Three Small UX Details That Made a Big Difference Ping-Pong Pair Mode (`) When you're bouncing between an editor and documentation (or two windows of the same app), checking Slack or WeChat once destroys normal MRU ordering. In AbcTab, pressing ` locks the highlighted app (or specific window) together with your current context as a pair: From then on, a single blind ⌘-Tab always snaps back to your paired target—even if you briefly jumped to other apps in between. Stopping a Stationary Cursor from Stealing Selection Because the switcher panel opens centered on screen, the mouse cursor often happens to sit right underneath one of the tiles. Early on, tiny trackpad micro-jitters would trigger hover selection and hijack ⌘-Tab. The fix in v1.4.0 was two-fold: Require >10pt of real pointer travel before hover selection arms itself, and re-suppress hover on any keypress. Add an explicit "Ignore mouse hover" toggle in General settings for pure-keyboard users (clicking a tile still works). Offline-First Licensing with Ed25519 I hate desktop utilities that phone home on every launch. AbcTab verifies licenses completely offline using an embedded Ed25519 public key (CryptoKit) against signed tokens—zero telemetry, zero background polling. AbcTab vs. AltTab: Honest Take If you rely on visual thumbnail previews and don't mind granting Screen Recording permission, AltTab is free, open-source, and genuinely great. If you'd rather avoid Screen Recording permission altogether and prefer keyboard-first letter jumping, Ping-Pong pairs, and Ghostty tab switching, you can read the full side-by-side breakdown here: 👉 AbcTab vs. AltTab — Full Comparison And if you want to try AbcTab yourself (macOS 14+, Apple Silicon & Intel, 14-day free trial with no credit card, $9.9 one-time lifetime license): 👉 Download AbcTab on SoloCraft Happy to answer any questions about Swift 6, AppKit panel focus quirks, or Accessibility API edge cases in the comments!

articles.title: Keeping secrets out of agent prompts: how Vault and DLP fit together
articles.description: Originally published on sandscale.dev. An agent that deploys code, queries a database or calls an API needs credentials. The usual shortcuts, a .env file in the repo, a key pasted into the prompt, a token in a shell history, put those credentials in places where they get copied. This post walks through how credentials leak in agent runs, what Sandscale's Vault and DLP each do about it, and which paths remain open. Everything about Sandscale below comes from sandscale.dev as of 20 November 2026. Where the docs are silent, we say so. How secrets leak in an agent run Think of the places a credential can end up: The prompt. A person pastes a key to help the agent along, or the agent reads a file that contains one and includes it in the next model call. From there it sits in a provider's logs and your own transcripts. Tool-call arguments. The agent builds a command or an API call that includes the key inline. Files and the repository. A .env file or a config with a token gets committed or copied. Command output. A tool prints the environment, or a debug log echoes a header. The output returns to the model as context. Logs and traces. Your own telemetry records the above. Lingering validity. The credential still works long after the run that needed it. No single control covers all six. Vault addresses the way a secret is delivered and how long it lasts. DLP addresses what leaves in prompts and tool calls. Neither inspects what the agent's own code does inside the box, and the end of this post is about that gap. Vault: deliver the secret without the model seeing it Sandscale's Vault works in three steps, as the site describes them: Store. You put a secret in Vault once, not in repos, prompts or environment files. Inject. It reaches the run in memory, never written to disk. End. It stops working when the run, session or lease ends. A run references a secret and Vault injects it at run time. Vault comes with every plan, Free included. Giving a sandbox a secret The step-by-step guide shows the flow. First store the secret in Vault (the guide shows the steps; the value is read without echoing it). Then reference it when you start a sandbox. With the TypeScript SDK: The sandbox gets DB_PASSWORD in its environment. Your code never handles the value. In the docs' words, the path is "the mount, data, then the secret's path". What the docs say happens to the value: Sandscale reads it as you, with your Vault permissions. If you may not read it, the start is refused with vault_env_refused and nothing starts. It goes to the sandbox only. It is never in the API's answer, a log, the run's record or the audit log. The audit entry names the variables, not the values. A start can name up to 50 values. Build host leases can carry secrets too, and they end with the lease. What an environment variable does and doesn't protect The secret reaches the sandbox as an environment variable. That keeps it out of your code, the API answer and the logs. It does not hide it from code running inside the sandbox: any process in the box can read its environment, including a command the agent runs. If the agent runs env or printenv, or a script prints its configuration, the value appears in that command's output. The agent over MCP When an agent connects over Sandscale's MCP server, it can list the names of your Vault secrets but cannot read their values. Every call runs as the signed-in person and lands in the audit log with the tool, region, outcome and app, never the arguments. An agent can know that app/db exists and ask for a sandbox that references it, without ever receiving the password. DLP: scan what leaves Vault handles the case where you do it right. DLP handles the case where someone does it wrong. Per the DLP page: Scan. Each prompt and MCP tool call is checked against built-in patterns and your own. Block. A credential or other sensitive value stops the call. Record. What was found, and where, goes into the audit log. The value itself does not. The headline claim on that page is that "a credential pasted into a prompt never reaches the model." It applies on every plan. Two things worth being straight about. First, pattern matching can only catch what the patterns describe. The docs say checks use "built-in and your own patterns", so a secret in an unusual format, or one an agent has transformed, is outside what a pattern catches until someone adds one. Second, the page describes scanning of prompts and MCP tool calls. It does not say that output coming back from a command is scanned, or that files written to disk are scanned. Putting the two together Leak path What covers it, per the docs What is not stated Key pasted into a prompt DLP scan blocks the call Coverage for unusual formats: only through patterns Key built into a tool call DLP scans MCP tool calls Scope beyond MCP tool calls Secret in repo or .env Vault: store once, not in repos or environment files Nothing stops someone writing a secret to a file Secret echoed in command output Not stated Whether output is scanned Secret in logs Vault: values never in logs or run record; audit names variables only Your own application logs inside the sandbox Credential valid after the run Vault: "stops working when the run, session or lease ends" Habits that help, whatever the tooling Use short-lived credentials where the system you call supports them. A leaked token that expires within an hour is a smaller problem. Scope them narrowly. Give the agent a read-only database role for a read-only task. Do not put credentials in prompts. DLP is a safety net, not a plan. Review the audit log after the first few runs. It records what DLP found, where, never the value, and the variable names Vault injected. Assume anything the agent can read, it can print. Design for that: if a secret must never reach the model, ask whether the agent needs the secret at all, or whether a narrower service call would do. Route risky actions through approvals, so a person confirms before an agent uses a credential for something irreversible. See approvals and agent policy. Where this leaves you Vault keeps the secret out of your code, the API answer, the logs and the model's context in the normal path. DLP catches the abnormal path, a secret typed or built into a prompt or a tool call. Between them they cover the main leak paths that happen before code runs. They do not turn the agent's own commands into a safe place to hold a secret, so the sandbox boundary, narrow credentials and review still matter. For the isolation side, see our post on isolating agent-run code. The audit log ties it together: every action is in a hash-chained log that every plan can read. Pricing shows what each plan includes; Vault and DLP are on all of them.

articles.title: Microsoft's agent-framework Package Was Hijacked on PyPI: What AI SaaS Teams Should Check
articles.description: On the evening of November 17, 2026 (UTC), two releases of Microsoft's official agent-framework package appeared on PyPI that did not come from the project's repository. Versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 carried a credential stealer that runs every time Python starts. Both are gone from PyPI, but anything that installed or cached them is still exposed. If you have a Python service that builds AI agents, or CI that installs Python dependencies without pins, this is a short check. Most teams were never on those versions. Those that were should rotate credentials today: the stealer targeted cloud identities, CI tokens and model provider keys. What Happened The GitHub advisory GHSA-764m-3ppc-5m73 lists the facts most sources agree on: Affected package: only the agent-framework meta-package on PyPI. Both bad versions pin agent-framework-core[all]==1.26.0, and Endor Labs checked 22 sibling agent-framework-* packages and found no new releases after November 12. Malicious versions: 1.26.1 (uploaded about 20:35 UTC) and 1.26.2 (about 21:08 UTC), both wheel-only. Last clean version: 1.26.0, published November 12. The advisory lists no newer patched release, and says 1.26.0 and earlier are not affected. Removal: both versions were removed from PyPI on the same evening. Sources disagree slightly on when 1.26.2 came down. Wiz says both were gone by 21:30 UTC. Note the second upload: 1.26.2 went up after 1.26.1 was pulled, so the publisher still had access then. Wiz says the attacker appears to have used a compromised client certificate for Microsoft's internal release pipeline, obtained in an unknown way. That root cause is Wiz's research. A project maintainer has reportedly confirmed the removal and an investigation, but Microsoft had published no advisory as of November 20. No npm or NuGet package was reported as compromised. The stealer collects npm and NuGet credentials; it did not spread there. How the Stealer Works The payload is a .pth file in site-packages. Python runs these at startup, so the stealer fires whenever any Python process starts there, pip included, without importing agent_framework. 1.26.1 added agent_framework_meta.pth, which loads agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py. 1.26.2 added af_runtime_diag.pth and a top-level af_runtime_diag.py, and restored the original __init__.py to make the change harder to spot. Per the advisory, Wiz and Endor Labs, it collects: environment variables whose names contain strings such as TOKEN, SECRET, KEY, AZURE, AWS, GITHUB, OPENAI, HF_, NPM and CI_, plus the environments of up to 300 other processes; credential files such as ~/.azure, .npmrc, .netrc, .git-credentials, .docker/config.json, pip.conf, Hugging Face tokens, and .env or JSON files under /app and /workspace; Azure managed-identity tokens for a dozen services, requested from the instance metadata endpoint; Azure DevOps pipeline tokens, and in 1.26.2, GitHub Actions OIDC tokens for jobs that have id-token: write. Everything was sent in one HTTP POST to a webhook.site URL. The published indicators include the user agents af-runtime-diagnostics/1 and runtime-diagnostics/1. Who Is Affected You installed agent-framework 1.26.1 or 1.26.2 anywhere: a laptop, a CI run, a container build or a server. Treat that environment as compromised. You run unpinned installs (pip install agent-framework or agent-framework>=1.x) and any build ran between about 20:35 and 21:30 UTC on November 17. Check whether it resolved a bad version. You use an internal package proxy or mirror (Artifactory, Nexus, a pip cache). It may have cached the bad wheels after PyPI removed them. You pin agent-framework==1.26.0 or earlier with a lockfile, or you only use agent-framework-core or the .NET packages: not affected by this incident. You do not use Microsoft Agent Framework at all: not affected. What to Do Today Search for the versions. Grep lockfiles (uv.lock, poetry.lock, requirements*.txt) and CI logs for agent-framework==1.26.1, 1.26.2, or agent_framework-1.26.1 / 1.26.2 wheel names. Include container images built since November 17. Look for the files without running Python. In each suspect environment, list site-packages with find or ls for agent_framework_meta.pth, af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. Endor Labs warns that running python or pip in an affected environment re-runs the stealer, so do not "just pip uninstall" first. Rebuild, do not clean. Throw away affected virtualenvs and images and rebuild from a clean base with agent-framework==1.26.0 pinned, ideally with hashes (pip install --require-hashes, or uv/Poetry lockfiles). Block the bad versions upstream. Add 1.26.1 and 1.26.2 to your package proxy's deny list so a cache cannot hand them out again. Rotate what the environment could read. Model provider keys (OpenAI, Azure OpenAI, Anthropic and others), cloud credentials, GitHub and npm tokens, PyPI tokens, Docker registry logins, Hugging Face tokens and database URLs in .env files. On a developer laptop, that includes the Azure CLI session and any saved git credentials. Remember that rotation does not revoke issued tokens. Managed-identity and OIDC tokens that were already stolen stay valid until they expire. Review what the identity could do while they lasted (Wiz notes up to 24 hours for the Azure tokens). How to Check Whether Anything Was Used Network logs: look for outbound requests to webhook.site from build agents or servers, and the user agents above. Cloud sign-ins: in Entra ID, review sign-ins and token use for managed identities and service principals after November 17, and check for new federated credentials or role assignments. GitHub: for workflows that installed 1.26.2 with id-token: write, check the cloud side of that trust (the AWS, Azure or GCP role it federates into) for actions you did not run. Review new deploy keys, personal access tokens and Actions secrets. Model providers: check usage dashboards for spend, models or API keys you do not recognise. Wiz reported that few of the requests it could observe at the exfiltration endpoint held real victim data. That is one team's view, not a reason to skip rotation. What This Says About Your Pipeline This came through the official package name and ran at install time. Three habits contain it: pin Python dependencies with hashes and let new releases age a few days; grant id-token: write only to deploy jobs, not install-and-test jobs (the GitHub Actions execution policies guide covers scoping); and keep production secrets out of build environments. What to Watch Next A Microsoft statement. Root cause and the state of the publishing credential stay unconfirmed until Microsoft says so. No other Microsoft package has been reported for this incident. The next agent-framework release. Before upgrading past 1.26.0, check it matches a tagged release in the repository. Copycats. Help Net Security places this among other 2026 attacks on AI tooling packages, which hold model and cloud credentials. Related Reading Shai-Hulud 2.0: The npm Worm Spreading Through SAP and Intercom Packages This Week Your AI Agent Needs Its Own Identity: A SaaS Access Blueprint TanStack Was Compromised Yesterday. Here's What SaaS Teams Need to Do Right Now. Next Step If steps 1 and 2 come back clean, only the pipeline hygiene above remains. If they find a bad version, or you cannot tell which secrets your build agents read, that is a production readiness question. The production readiness upgrade covers dependency pinning, CI identity scoping and secret placement. Bring your lockfiles, your CI workflow files and a list of where your provider keys live.
